scenario: At the end of your shift you ordered a blood test and CT* scan for one of your patients, Mrs Tao, who was complaining of feeling faint and confused following surgery. The investigation results need to be reviewed tonight otherwise Mrs Tao’s treatment may be delayed. You have just arrived home and realise you forgot to hand over the need to review the investigation results to the FY1 doctor taking over your shift. You have been unable to contact the FY1 taking over directly.
options: Telephone the ward nursing staff and ask them to get the FY1 taking over your shift to  look up the investigation results
Contact the on-call specialty trainee (registrar)* and explain the situation
Go back to the hospital and look up the investigation results yourself
Contact an FY1 colleague working on another ward to ask her to look up the investigation results for you
Review the investigation results first thing in the morning when your shift starts

scenario: You work on the Breast Surgery unit. Because of recent advances in surgical techniques, inpatient stay has dropped from five days to an overnight stay. The bed numbers on your ward have reduced and you have found you have some free time available. However, the number of learning opportunities has also reduced as a result.
options: Take on a position of responsibility in the doctors’ common room committee
Ask the Foundation Programme Director if you can move to another firm
Ask your consultant if you can be scheduled for outpatient clinics and theatre sessions
Offer to assist your FY1 colleagues on other busier wards
Inform the Foundation Programme Director that the job should be re-assessed for training

scenario: On a ward round, the specialty trainee (registrar)* tells you to write a drug prescription for a patient. Before prescribing the drug you realise that this medicine is contra-indicated with the patient’s other treatments. The specialty trainee (registrar) has now left the ward.
options: Write up the drug as requested but omit the start date for the drug until you are able to speak to the specialty trainee (registrar)
Ask another senior colleague for advice on whether a different drug should be prescribed
Decline from prescribing the drug but write in the patient notes that the drug is contra-indicated in this patient
Discuss with the ward pharmacist the most appropriate drug to prescribe instead
Try to contact the specialty trainee (registrar) to inform him of the patient’s other treatments

scenario: Whilst taking a history from a new patient, she tells you that she was sexually abused by her father as a child but has since come to terms with this. Later she mentions that her father is looking after her eight year old daughter while she is in hospital. You explain that you will have to inform Social Services of the possible risk to her daughter. She says that she would not leave her daughter at risk and insists that the information she has given you remains confidential.
options: Offer to telephone her father to check that her daughter is ok
Discuss what you should do with the nurse in charge of the ward
Discuss what you should do with your clinical supervisor*
Explain that it is your duty to discuss this with Social Services as her daughter may be at risk
Agree to keep the information confidential but suggest that she try and find alternative caring arrangements for her daughter

scenario: A patient with a complex medical history dies on the ward after a prolonged period of investigation and treatment. Although enough is known to be able to complete a death certificate, your consultant is keen to arrange a post mortem to find out more. He gains the consent of the patient’s family for this. However, shortly afterwards the family speak to you as you are passing on the ward. They tell you they felt coerced into saying ‘yes’ to the post mortem and are upset about the request.
options: Refer the family’s request  back to your consultant and ask him to speak to them again
Ask your consultant for his reasons for requesting the post mortem
Ask another senior colleague within the team to meet with the family to discuss their concerns
Explore the family’s concerns with them
Reassure the family that post mortems are standard practice in situations like these

scenario: At your morning briefing you are informed by Infection Control* that all hospital staff must roll their sleeves up when they have any clinical interaction with patients. During your shift you notice that your FY1 colleague always has her sleeves down.
options: Tell Infection Control* that your colleague is not complying with their policy
Speak directly to your FY1 colleague about your observation
Raise your observation with to the nurse in charge of the ward
Do not say anything immediately but monitor the situation over the course of the next few days
Discuss the situation with your specialty trainee (registrar)*

scenario: It is 8am and you are beginning a New Year’s Day shift. A fellow FY1 colleague has called in sick for the same shift; stating that she has food poisoning. The following day you learn that your absent colleague had posted pictures on a social networking site from a New Year’s Eve party that she had attended the night before her shift.
options: Make other colleagues on the rota aware of the photos from the party
Suggest to your  FY1 colleague that she remove the photos from the social networking site
Seek advice from another FY1 colleague
Ask your colleague for an explanation of why she called in sick the day after a party
Alert a senior colleague to the photos on the social networking site

scenario: The specialty trainee (registrar)* on your ward, Dr Kitson, is a good friend of yours. She has just sent you a text saying she is running 30 minutes late for work and asks you to cover for her. One of the patients on the ward, Mr Bradley, informs you that Dr Kitson was supposed to be discharging him first thing that morning and it is now 9am. He explains that it is urgent he gets to work by 10am and it is a 45 minute journey to get there.
options: Sign Mr Bradley’s discharge paperwork yourself
Explain to Mr Bradley that Dr Kitson has been delayed so he may want to contact his work and let them know the situation
Contact Dr Kitson and find out whether she can give verbal approval to the discharge
Find another senior colleague in your team to review and discharge Mr Bradley
Offer Mr Bradley the option of signing a self-discharge form

scenario: Mr Farmer has been a patient on the ward for six months; he has a tracheostomy and he breathes with the aid of a ventilator following a traumatic brain injury.  As you make your rounds, you notice Mr Farmer appears to be experiencing breathing problems.  Both the consultant and specialty trainee (registrar)* are dealing with a patient on the neighbouring ward.  This is your first week and you have not yet attended a potentially critically unwell patient by yourself.
options: Call the crash team to attend to Mr Farmer as a matter of urgency
Seek advice from the physiotherapy team who are on the ward and have experience in managing Mr Farmer’s case
Contact the specialty trainee (registrar)* to discuss Mr Farmer’s symptoms
Ask the ward nurse to fully assess Mr Farmer’s status with you immediately
Ask the consultant to return to your ward straight away to attend to Mr Farmer

scenario: It is 6pm and you are clerking a patient who is to undergo an elective splenectomy the next morning. Before he left, your consultant asked you before he left to prescribe the antibiotics and immunisations that need to be given that evening so that surgery can proceed tomorrow. You now cannot find the folder containing the pre-operative protocols and there is no intranet version. Your consultant has already gone home.
options: Seek advice from the on-call microbiologist
Look in the British National Formulary* and prescribe what is suggested
Find a protocol on the internet from a local hospital
Ask the nurse in charge of the ward what is normally given
Seek advice from the surgical specialty trainee (registrar)*

scenario: Your consultant has to attend to a patient on another ward. In her absence she asks you to liaise with the radiology department to arrange an urgent CT* scan for Mrs Lewis.  You provide a written request to book the test but are contacted by the radiologist a few hours later. He informs you that he has rejected your request on the basis of insufficient information.
options: Take the CT scan request form to another radiologist
Ask the radiologist to explain in more detail what was missing from the request
Ask your specialty trainee (registrar)* to discuss the request with the radiologist
Call your consultant to inform her that the radiologist has rejected the request
Ask your consultant to return to your ward so you can explain the situation

scenario: On the morning ward round, your specialty trainee (registrar)* said that Mrs Anderson is medically fit following her total knee replacement and could be discharged if the occupational therapist* feels it is appropriate. The Occupational therapist* has assessed Mrs Anderson and believes it is safe for her to go home with a care package that has been arranged. It is now 4pm and the nurse informs you that Mrs Anderson is demanding to see a doctor as she does not feel that she is ready to go home yet. An elective admission is waiting in the day room for Mrs Anderson's bed.
options: Ask Mrs Anderson about her concerns
Ask a senior colleague to speak with Mrs Anderson
Ask the bed manager if he can find another bed for the elective patient
Explain to Mrs Anderson that the bed has already been allocated and she has to go home
Ask the Occupational therapist* to come and speak to Mrs Anderson with you

scenario: Mr Reese has end-stage respiratory failure and needs continuous oxygen therapy. While you are taking an arterial blood gas sample, he confides in you that he knows he is dying and he really wants to die at home. He has not told anyone else about this as he thinks it will upset his family, and the nursing staff who are looking after him so well.
options: Tell Mr Reese that whilst he is on oxygen therapy he will need to stay in hospital
Reassure Mr Reese that the team will take account of his wishes
Discuss his case with the multi-disciplinary team*
Discuss with Mr Reese's family his wish to die at home
Discuss Mr Reese's home circumstances with his General Practitioner

scenario: Your consultant Dr Jackson has asked you to prescribe a second antibiotic for a patient who has a chest infection which has been slow to respond to initial treatment. Later that day, you are contacted by a specialist trainee in microbiology who informs you that the new antibiotic is not in the hospital formulary. She tells you that the new antibiotic should not be used because of the risk of clostridium difficile infection.
options: Prescribe what the microbiology trainee advises
Explain that Dr Jackson requested the antibiotic and he would be the best person to speak to about the prescription
Agree to contact Dr Jackson to discuss the prescription
Suggest that the microbiology trainee reviews the patient herself in order to be able to make an informed decision
Do not change the prescription and make a record in the notes of the microbiology trainee's concerns

scenario: You are just finishing a busy shift on the Acute Assessment Unit (AAU). Your FY1 colleague who is due to replace you for the evening shift leaves a message with the nurse in charge that she will be 15 to 30 minutes late. There is only a 30 minute overlap between your timetables to handover to your colleague. You need to leave on time as you have a social engagement to attend with your partner.
options: Make a list of the patients under your care on the AAU, detailing their outstanding issues, leaving this on the notice board in the doctors’ office when your shift ends and then leave at the end of your shift
Quickly go around each of the patients on the AAU, leaving an entry in the notes highlighting the major outstanding issues relating to each patient and then leave at the end of your shift
Make a list of patients and outstanding investigations to give to your colleague as soon as she arrives

Ask your specialty trainee (registrar)* if you can leave a list of your patients and their outstanding issues with him to give to your colleague when she arrives and then leave at the end of your shift
Leave a message for your partner explaining that you will be 30 minutes late

scenario: You are looking after Mr Kucera who has previously been treated for prostate carcinoma. Preliminary investigations are strongly suggestive of a recurrence. As you finish taking blood from a neighbouring patient, Mr Kucera leans across and says “tell me honestly, is my cancer back?”
options: Explain to Mr Kucera that it is likely that his cancer has come back
Reassure Mr Kucera that he will be fine
Explain to Mr Kucera that you do not have all the test results, but you will speak to him as soon as you do
Inform Mr Kucera that you will chase up the results of his tests and ask one of your  senior colleagues to discuss them with him
Invite Mr Kucera to join you and a senior nurse in a quiet room, get a colleague to hold your ‘bleep’ then explore his fears

scenario: You have been approached by a FY1 colleague, James, who has been on shifts with another FY1 doctor, Mark, for the last two weeks. James tells you that Mark has gradually become increasingly careless in monitoring and documenting patient records. On three occasions, James tells you that he has found Mark asleep in the common room whilst on duty. You know Mark very well and have never witnessed such behaviour when you have worked with him previously.
options: Tell James that you have never witnessed such behaviour from Mark
Suggest to James that he speaks to Mark directly about his concerns
Advise James to document his concerns
Inform a senior colleague about what James has told you
Tell James you will speak to Mark about his behaviour
Ask other members of the team whether they have witnessed this behaviour in Mark
Advise James to speak to a senior colleague about his concerns
Ask James whether he has any evidence that patient safety is being compromised

scenario: You have been prescribed codeine for persistent back pain which has become worse in the last few weeks. You have noticed that during shifts you are becoming increasingly tired, finding it difficult to concentrate and your performance, as a result, has been less effective.
options: Ask a colleague to assist with your workload until you finish your codeine prescription
Make an effort to increase the number of breaks during your next shift
Stop taking the codeine immediately
Make an appointment to see your General Practitioner
Seek advice from a specialist consultant about your back pain
Arrange to speak with your specialty trainee (registrar)* before your next shift and make them aware of your situation
Seek advice from your clinical supervisor* regarding further support
Consider taking some annual leave

scenario: You are reviewing one of your patients, Mrs Hobbs, who is on your ward being treated for an infection in her toe. During a routine examination you notice that in Mrs Hobbs’ drug chart the FY2 has prescribed her penicillin and the administration is due in 45 minutes time. You remember your consultant informing you earlier that day that Mrs Hobbs was allergic to penicillin.
options: Inform the FY2 that they have made an error
Cross out the prescription on Mrs Hobbs’ drug chart, dating and initialling the amendment
Tell the nursing staff on duty not to administer penicillin to Mrs Hobbs
Contact your specialty trainee (registrar)* to confirm what the consultant has said about the penicillin allergy
Inform your consultant about the situation
Ask Mrs Hobbs whether she is allergic to penicillin
Explain to Mrs Hobbs that an incorrect prescription has been made by the FY2
Review Mrs Hobbs notes to try and clarify whether she is allergic to penicillin

scenario: You are a FY1 doctor working in the Emergency Department (ED). A 48 year old patient presents with an ankle injury. He is intoxicated, loud and demands immediate medical treatment. There are four patients waiting ahead of him.  He is upsetting the other patients and at one point, threatens another patient with physical violence.
options: Ask one of the nurses to try and calm the patient down
Call security for assistance
Tell the patient that his behaviour is inappropriate and will not be tolerated
Arrange for the patient to be moved to a side room away from the other patients
Arrange for the patient to be treated as soon as possible
Tell the patient he will not be treated if he continues to behave in this manner
Ensure the other patients are not distressed by the situation
Ask the other patients if they would mind if this patient was treated before them

scenario: You are assisting on a ward one afternoon when you notice that a patient has two tablets in his hands that he is about to consume. The medication was prescribed to him earlier this morning and his case notes clearly state ‘take one tablet twice daily’. The patient in question does not speak English.
options: Arrange for a translator to ask the patient if he knows how he is supposed to take the medication
Prevent him from taking both tablets now
Speak to the doctor who prescribed the medication about the incident
Illustrate on a piece of paper how and when to take the medication
Seek advice on drug dosing from the pharmacist
Inform the nurse in charge about the incident
Find out if his relatives speak good English and can translate the prescription to the patient
Ask the nurse who dispensed the medication to explain why he has more tablets than prescribed

scenario: You have just started your shift. You have not met one of the patients, Mrs Gordon but you know that she is being treated for a fractured knee and is recovering well. Her husband has noticed that she has lots of bruising around her knee. He angrily approaches you claiming her doctor is not doing her job properly as the bruising is getting worse.
options: Ask a senior colleague to speak to Mr Gordon
Ask the nurse who has been caring for Mrs Gordon to speak with him
Ask Mr Gordon to lower his voice as he is disrupting the other patients
Tell Mr Gordon the other doctor has now finished her shift so you are now taking over responsibility for Mrs Gordon
Try to answer any questions Mr Gordon has
Reassure Mr Gordon that the bruising will be the result of the fractured knee
Set up an appointment for Mr Gordon to meet with the consultant
Re-examine Mrs Gordon’s knee

scenario: You become aware that one of your FY1 colleagues, Daniel, is consistently not doing his fair share of the ward work. His night shift colleague has told you that he leaves much of the routine work for her and provides poor handover information. However he is personally very likeable and always performs jobs diligently when directly requested. You know that no-one has broached this with him yet.
options: Discuss Daniel’s behaviour with his clinical supervisor*
Suggest to the nursing staff that they ask Daniel directly to complete the routine work
Explain to Daniel that his behaviour means colleagues have to do extra work and this could impact on patient safety
Bring up the issue of effective handovers at the next team meeting
Ask Daniel if he needs help with his handover
Discuss the situation with your consultant
Ask other staff on the ward if they are experiencing problems with Daniel
Suggest to your night shift colleague that she speaks to Daniel directly about him not completing his tasks

scenario: It is the end of your shift and on your way out of the ward you remind one of the nurses that Mr Baker, who has been admitted to the hospital with chest pains, needs his blood taken within the hour for cardiac markers. The nurse tells you that the ward has now got very busy so Mr Baker will have to wait. She is very abrupt in her response to you.
options: Ask the nurse for further details about the other urgent tasks that need to be completed on the ward
Ask the FY1 taking over your shift to take Mr Baker’s blood
Discuss with the nurse in charge the procedure for taking essential bloods at busy times
Insist that the nurse tries to find the time to take Mr Baker’s bloods
Take Mr Baker’s blood yourself
Suggest to the nurse that she considers how she speaks to other members of the team in future
The next day, speak to the nurse privately about the way she spoke to you
Speak to the nurse in charge about the way the nurse spoke to you

scenario: A confused patient has intra-abdominal infection and acute renal failure after a procedure. Instructions to the nursing staff are clearly written in the notes regarding what action to take in response to a change in the patient’s urine output. On the morning ward round you find these instructions were not followed by the night nursing team and the patient has deteriorated as a consequence. You immediately ensure the patient is treated appropriately.
options: Inform the nurse in charge of the ward of the incident
Explain to the patient that there was an error with the management of her condition
Inform a senior member of the medical team of the incident
Speak to the nurses involved next time you see them about your concerns with their management of the patient
Find out whether the nurses were aware of the instructions regarding changes to the patients urine output
Offer to write a protocol formalising team communication
Record your account of the nights events in the patient's notes
Ask the nurses to increase the frequency of observations on the patient

scenario: You are treating Mrs Taylor for a urinary infection. You receive the antibiotic sensitivity results. You inform your consultant that the E coli causing Mrs Taylor’s urinary infection is sensitive to amoxicillin. As a result, this antibiotic is then started. You realise later that day that you have misread the result and that the E coli is actually resistant to amoxicillin and is sensitive only to ciprofloxacin. Mrs Taylor had no adverse reaction to the antibiotic.
options: Inform your consultant of the correct result
Record the incident as a learning point in your learning portfolio*
Contact microbiology for advice
Tell Mrs Taylor that you have prescribed the incorrect antibiotic
Reassess Mrs Taylor’s vital signs
Change the antibiotic to ciprofloxacin
Repeat the urine specimen culture
Ask your specialty trainee (registrar)* for advice

scenario: You have worked on a ward with another FY1 colleague, Ben, for the last three weeks. You have noticed that Ben seems to avoid writing prescriptions and filling in drug charts. The nurses appear to be getting frustrated with Ben because of this. When you speak to Ben about it, he tells you that he is dyslexic but has not told anyone as he is embarrassed.
options: Make the nursing staff aware of the situation
Check all the drug charts and prescriptions Ben has recently written
Explain to Ben the potential safety risks to patients if he continues to ignore the issue
Discuss the situation with a senior colleague
Recommend to Ben that he raises this with his educational supervisor*
Offer to help Ben with his prescriptions and drug charts
Discuss the situation with your team and ask them to help you monitor Ben’s drug charts and prescriptions
Speak to occupational health* about the best course of action to take

scenario: You review a patient on the surgical ward who has had an appendicectomy done earlier on the day. You write a prescription for strong painkillers. The staff nurse challenges your decision and refuses to give the medication to the patient.
options: Instruct the nurse to give the medication to the patient
Discuss with the nurse why she disagrees with the prescription
Ask a senior colleague for advice
Complete a clinical incident form
Cancel the prescription on the nurse’s advice
Arrange to speak to the nurse later to discuss your working relationship
Write in the medical notes that the nurse has declined to give the medication
Review the case again

scenario: A 45 year old alcoholic is admitted in the afternoon with delirium tremens after stopping drinking two days previously. During the night you are called to see him as he has become very aggressive and is demanding to be allowed home.  As you arrive on the ward he punches one of the nurses. He is confused, shouting and threatening other patients.
options: Prescribe extra sedation for the patient
Ask the nursing staff to call hospital security
Attempt to talk to the patient to try and calm him down
Reassure the other patients in the ward that they are safe
Ask the nursing staff to help you restrain the patient
Ask the nursing staff to call the police
Inform the patient that his behaviour is inappropriate and will not be tolerated
Ensure that the nurse who was punched is not badly injured

scenario: At lunch a FY1 colleague bursts into tears. She says she feels she is not coping with the job. She thinks that her consultant is too demanding and the nurses are annoyed because she is not keeping up with the workload.
options: Talk to her about the circumstances of her distress
Suggest she discusses the issues with her specialty trainee (registrar)*
Advise her to take a few days annual leave to rest
Encourage her to seek some counselling
Offer to go with her to talk to her consultant
Inform her educational supervisor* that she appears to be struggling
Ask other members of the team to be supportive as she is having difficulties coping
Offer to assist with some of her workload

scenario: Your consultant Dr Pisani calls you on the phone and asks you to prescribe a sedative for an in-patient with a pneumonia who is  distressed. He had intended to do this during the ward round but forgot. You check the dose in the BNF* and notice that the appropriate dose is half that advised by your consultant. You double check with your Clinical Pharmacist who agrees that the dose prescribed by Dr Pisani is inappropriately high. The ward nurses tell you that Dr Pisani usually prescribes that dose for his patients and they have never had any problems. appropriate; 5= Least appropriate).
options: Prescribe the dose as written in the BNF and corroborated by the Clinical pharmacist
Ask a senior to review the need of sedation in this patient until you clarify with the consultant
Ask the Clinical pharmacist to contact the Consultant to clarify the dose
Contact Dr Pisani directly yourself to discuss the prescription
Prescribe the dose advised by Dr Pisani

scenario: A nurse on your ward tells you that she has just administered intravenous metoclopramide to one of your patients.  However, when she was discarding the drug phial, she realised that the date on the phial showed that it had expired.  The patient has not developed any adverse symptoms till now.
options: Explain and apologise to the patient about the mistake
Write an incident report and send it to the office in charge of adverse drug events
Tell the nurse that there is no need to report the incident as the patient has come to no harm
Review the patient the next morning  to ensure that no new symptoms have developed
Ask the nurse to give a repeat dose of metoclopramide, making sure that the new dose is not expired
Advise the patient to remind the nurses to check the expiry dates on any drug he is given from now on
Inform the Nurse-in-charge about the incident
Find time to check the expiry dates on all drugs in the ward yourself

scenario: You are called to review a 65 year old male on the ward. He had been admitted the day before for investigation of intractable low back pain for which he has been on NSAIDs*. He is now complaining of severe abdominal pain and distension. On examination you notice that he looks pale and is very tender all over the abdomen.
options: Prescribe glycerine suppositories
Arrange for an urgent erect chest x-ray
Take urgent bloods whilst establishing intravenous access
Start him on intravenous hyoscine butylbromide
Keep the patient on oral fluids only
Start an opiate analgesic to relieve the pain
Organise an urgent US of the abdomen
Ask the bed manager to immediately transfer to a surgical ward

scenario: You are called to see a patient with respiratory distress. He is a 76 year old male who was admitted with acute exacerbation of COPD. His heart rate is 100/ minute, regular, BP* is 150/85 and oxygen saturation is 88% on air. He is conscious but tachypnoeic and distressed.
options: Immediately give the patient high flow oxygen.
Take an arterial blood gas.
Administer IV* aminophylline.
Give the patient 24% oxygen until you assess further.
Administer a benzodiazepine to calm him down.

scenario: You are covering a ward out of hours. An FY2 doctor, Jeremy tells you that he will be back shortly. As the ward becomes busier, you note that Jeremy has not returned from his break. You find Jeremy asleep in the break room. You are very busy and becoming overwhelmed on the ward, so you decide to wake Jeremy. Jeremy tells you to leave him alone as he needs the rest.
options: Explain to Jeremy that you feel overwhelmed, under pressure and need his support
Explain to Jeremy that his behaviour is inappropriate
Leave Jeremy to sleep and carry on alone throughout the shift
Ask other colleagues on the ward for their support
Inform a more senior colleague that you are not receiving the support that you need from your FY2
Decide to work late to finish the tasks
rationale: This is a very appropriate action. It is clear and explicit that you need help on the ward, as you cannot manage the workload alone, whilst remaining polite and professional. It does not cast judgement on why Jeremy is sleeping, but simply asks for his help now that he is awake.

This action is somewhat appropriate. Although staff members are entitled to take breaks and rest, which may even include a small nap, this must not over run to when they are meant to be performing clinical duties. However, the response is not entirely appropriate as although Jeremy's behaviour is inappropriate, it does not explain to him what your immediate concerns are with the busy ward and that his help is needed now.

This is an inappropriate action. Regardless of Jeremy's reasons for taking a nap, when his allotted break time has finished, Jeremy should be ready to continue his clinical duties. If he is unwell or has genuine reasons, then the situation can be escalated, so that he can be sent home and appropriate cover can be found. However, by leaving him to sleep, the situation is not being dealt with, and it also means that the clinical work is becoming overwhelming for one FY1 doctor. Additionally, patient safety may be at risk due to not enough staff and support available.

This action is somewhat appropriate. It is recognising your own limitations and that you are becoming overwhelmed and require support on the ward. Asking for help is a positive step and ensures patient safety. However, the colleagues on the ward may have other duties and asking for their help is taking them away from their own work and it hasn't dealt with the main problem at this time, which is Jeremy sleeping and not able to perform his own duties.

This is a very appropriate action. Escalating the situation appropriately has two benefits: it means that additional support can be found for you in order to carry out the jobs properly, and patient safety isn't compromised. It also means that a senior colleague can deal sensitively with Jeremy, as there may be more complex issues involved that may explain the reasons why he is so tired and unable to complete his shift, which can be dealt with by his senior.

This is an inappropriate action. Despite the good intentions behind working late to get the jobs completed, it is inappropriate because, as an individual, you cannot simply take on an entire colleague's workload. You will be tired after a long shift, and in these circumstances mistakes can happen. Rest periods are essential, so you need to finish your shift when allocated and get the appropriate rest needed, so that you are ready for your next shift. Safe working times and rotas have been designed with this in mind. Working late to finish tasks also sets a precedent for other doctors to do the same. Any leftover jobs can be safely handed over to the on-call team or postponed until the following day. Finally, by working late to finish the tasks, not only might it be unsafe, but it is not dealing with the problem that you have been unsupported by a team member, Jeremy, who is asleep, and these needs escalating appropriately.

scenario: Jeremy remains asleep for the remainder of the shift. As you are leaving, Jeremy wakes up and tells you that, before that shift, he had not slept in 4 days. He commends you for managing well without him. Later on, you find out that your colleague, Shannon, has also had a previous similar experience with Jeremy.
options: Ask Jeremy why he is struggling to sleep during his time off
Tell Jeremy that he is putting patients at risk by coming to work over-tired
Encourage Jeremy to seek support from his General Practitioner (GP)
Advise Jeremy that you think it is inappropriate to sleep whilst on shift
rationale: This is a compassionate approach, understanding that there are likely to be reasons why Jeremy has been sleeping on his shifts. As an individual, you may not be able to fix the reasons on your own, and you will still need to escalate the situation, but by showing an empathetic and compassionate response to a fellow colleague, you are more likely to get a positive response from Jeremy, and foster trust and positive working relationship in future.

This is a very appropriate action. Whatever the reasons are for Jeremy being so tired that he needs to sleep through his shift, in doing so, he is risking patient safety. If he has genuine reasons, these need to be escalated and dealt with appropriately and he may require a period of sick or compassionate leave before he is safe to work again.

This is a kind and compassionate approach, taking into consideration that there may be genuine reasons why Jeremy is sleeping during a shift and these reasons need addressing, as he is currently not safe to be at work. Encouraging Jeremy to seek support from his GP is a compassionate and empathetic approach by directing him to get some help, rather than cast judgments on his behaviour.

Although it is inappropriate for Jeremy to sleep whilst on shift (not in his allocated break time), advising him that you think his behaviour is inappropriate is somewhat unhelpful, as it might be interpreted as inflammatory by Jeremy and cause a breakdown in trust. This action does not offer any practical solutions, such as speaking with a senior colleague or healthcare professional, nor does it highlight to Jeremy the additional stress that it has put you under, which has meant that jobs on the ward are not completed and thus patient safety may be compromised.

scenario: You are working in the Emergency Department, and you notice that your consultant, Julia, is failing to wash her hands ahead of conducting physical examinations of patients. You are aware that this is standard protocol. Later that day, you are in the break room when you overhear Julia discussing with another senior colleague that she had a spray tan that morning before work and cannot get her skin wet today as it may make the tan uneven.
options: Julia could be spreading bacteria between patients by not washing her hands
Julia is discussing her spray tan with a senior colleague
Julia is putting herself at risk by not washing her hands after seeing patients
Patients may notice that Julia is not washing her hands
That you are not directly involved in the conversation
rationale: This is a very important consideration. The standard protocols to wash hands exist for the primary purpose of preventing bacteria spreading between patients and other staff. Washing hands is a critical element in preventing transmission of bacteria between patients and staff and also in preventing the development of resistant bacteria. In being a healthcare professional, first and foremost, it is important that you are not causing any harm.

This consideration is not important at all. What Julia does in her own time and who she chooses to discuss it with, is not important. Having a spray tan is not prohibited, the issue here is solely that Julia is not washing hands, and in doing so, is not following Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) protocols and potentially putting herself and patients at risk.

This is a very important consideration. Not only is Julia putting her patients at risk by touching them without washing her hands, she is also risking spreading bacteria and therefore illnesses to others and herself. It is very important to ensure that it is safe to oneself as the medical professional, before approaching a patient. By not appropriately cleaning her hands (or wearing gloves) before and after conducting physical examination of patients, Julia is putting herself at risk.

This is a very important consideration. As well as endangering herself and patients by potentially transmitting bacteria, she is setting a bad example to colleagues and patients. Patients will likely lose trust in her and other medical staff members if they can't be trusted to do basic measures of Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) well. The ramifications of this loss of trust could be significant. It could also lead to complaints about the individual doctor, department and hospital.

This consideration is not important at all. Once noticed, it doesn't matter what the reason is for Julia not washing her hands, or whether you are directly involved in that discussion. The most important aspect is that Julia is not washing her hands and in doing so, she is putting patients, colleagues and herself at risk.

scenario: During a busy night shift, you ask your FY1 colleague, James, to complete a blood test for one of your patients, Mr Rowley. You introduce James to Mr Rowley and shortly after James begins to complete the blood test, and you leave. After waiting a few hours, the blood test results are still not back. You call the laboratory, who state that they have no blood test results for a Mr Rowley, but state that there are results for a different patient on your ward. You have repeated the blood sample for Mr Rowley and sent these to the laboratory. You know that no other patient on your ward has recently had a blood test, so you feel sure that James has labelled the blood test wrong.
options: Inform James that he has labelled Mr Rowley's blood test wrong
Encourage James to double check the labelling of blood tests in the future
Explain to James that the laboratory has stated that they have no blood tests for a Mr Rowley
Ask James if he remembers labelling Mr Rowley's blood tests
Suggest to James that he gets someone to check over his labelling of blood tests in future
Tell James that you will not ask him to complete blood tests for your patients again
Inform James that Mr Rowley will not be very happy with him
Tell James that he has wasted the laboratory's time
rationale: It is clear from the details in the stem that it is highly likely that James has incorrectly labelled the blood samples. This is a mistake, but it can be easily done and most importantly any mistake is learnt from. You have already resent the samples so the important thing for patient safety has already been done. Therefore, this question is asking about what happens next. Option B, C and D are the most appropriate actions to take. Option B is appropriate as by asking James to double check the labelling in future, you are alerting James to the probable error that he has made in a non-judgemental way. Option C is also appropriate as you are explaining to James that the laboratory has not received any samples for Mr Rowley, which allows James to come to the same conclusion himself that he had made a mistake and incorrectly labelled the samples. It is factual and non-judgemental, but it is not shying away from explaining to James what has happened. Option D is also appropriate, as you are opening channels of communication with James in a non-judgemental way. Asking James if he can remember the details might prompt him to realise the error and address it directly. Although it is likely that James has incorrectly labelled the samples, option A does not help him address the mistake. Option E is somewhat patronising and not helpful to James and does not address the issue directly. Option F is an over exaggeration to a small mistake, that many professionals will make. Option G may not be true and is likely to upset James unnecessarily. Option H is again unhelpful, as it does not help him to address the mistake and learn from it.

scenario: You are working in the Emergency Department and have just reviewed a 10 year old boy with a probable diagnosis of appendicitis. You attempt to contact the surgical registrar/specialty trainee several times, and when he responds, he is very rude and states that "just like all the other FY1 doctors, you are unable to use your knowledge to make the right decisions". You have never had an interaction with him before, but your FY1 colleagues have said that he can be very rude.
options: "I am sorry to disturb you, but I am worried about this patient"
"Can you explain why you feel that I have made a wrong decision?"
"Would you like me to explain why I bleeped you?"
"I feel that you are being very rude"
"My FY1 colleagues have said that you are very rude"
rationale: Incivility amongst colleagues can be difficult to manage and upsetting to be on the receiving end of. However, the most important thing in the short-term is the safety of the patient. Unprofessional behaviour needs be dealt with, but this can be done later and separately if needed. It is important to diffuse any potential arguments and keep the conversation professional and patient centred. Option A is the most appropriate thing to say as it is polite, professional, but gets to the point that you are worried about this patient, who is the priority in this situation. Option C is an appropriate response, as it is polite and reiterates that there is a purpose to you bleeping him regarding patient care and that you need to explain this. Option B is a somewhat appropriate response. Although it is opening the dialogue, it does not appear from the information that we have been given, that the wrong decision has been made, therefore inviting self-criticism is unlikely to be helpful for the patient or help building relationships going forward. Option D is not an appropriate response as although you think that he has been rude, telling him in this moment is unlikely to move the conversation forward and has lost track of the patient focus. Option E is the least appropriate thing to say, as it implies that people are gossiping behind his back and is likely to escalate tensions between you and the surgical registrar/specialty trainee. This response has also lost sight of patient care.

scenario: A 72-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target INR 2.0-3.0) presents with haematemesis and melaena. His INR is 6.8 and he is hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Withhold warfarin and recheck INR in 24 hours
IV vitamin K alone
IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
Fresh frozen plasma alone
Oral vitamin K and observe
explanation: Major bleeding on warfarin with a high INR requires urgent reversal with IV vitamin K AND PCC (or FFP if PCC unavailable). Withholding alone is too slow for active bleeding.

scenario: A patient on therapeutic-dose LMWH develops a large bruise at the injection site but no other bleeding. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop the LMWH immediately
Give protamine sulfate
Reassure and continue, monitoring for other bleeding
Switch to unfractionated heparin
Check APTT and adjust the dose
explanation: A local injection-site bruise is common and not an indication to stop anticoagulation. Reassure, continue, and monitor for signs of significant bleeding.

scenario: A 58-year-old man has central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm with sweating and nausea for 40 minutes. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Aspirin and observe for 6 hours
Aspirin, then urgent primary PCI
GTN spray and discharge if pain settles
Troponin and discharge if normal
CT coronary angiogram
explanation: ST-elevation MI is a time-critical emergency — activate the primary PCI pathway immediately. Aspirin is given but the priority is reperfusion.

scenario: A 65-year-old man has sudden severe 'tearing' chest pain radiating to the back, with a BP difference of 30 mmHg between arms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome
Pulmonary embolism
Aortic dissection
Pericarditis
Gastro-oesophageal reflux
explanation: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back with a pulse/BP differential between arms is classic for aortic dissection — a surgical emergency.

scenario: A 70-year-old woman has an irregularly irregular pulse, rate 110, and is haemodynamically stable. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
options: Synchronised DC cardioversion
IV amiodarone
Rate control with a beta-blocker and assess stroke risk
Digoxin loading
Immediate anticoagulation only
explanation: In stable AF, rate control (beta-blocker/CCB) is first-line, and stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) determines anticoagulation. Cardioversion is for unstable or recent-onset AF.

scenario: A 60-year-old man has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm. He is hypotensive and dizzy. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Adenosine 6 mg IV
Synchronised DC cardioversion
IV metoprolol
Vagal manoeuvres and observe
IV amiodarone
explanation: An unstable tachyarrhythmia (hypotension, dizziness) requires synchronised DC cardioversion, not drugs. Adenosine is for stable SVT.

scenario: A 45-year-old man with a stab wound to the abdomen is hypotensive, tachycardic, with cool peripheries. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: IV crystalloid bolus and urgent surgery
IV inotropes
CT abdomen before surgery
Observe with serial Hb
Oral fluids
explanation: Haemorrhagic shock from trauma needs rapid IV fluid/blood resuscitation and urgent surgical control of the bleeding source. Do not delay surgery for imaging.

scenario: A septic patient is hypotensive with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: IV antibiotics only
Blood cultures, IV antibiotics and IV fluids within 1 hour
IV fluids only
Inotropes first
CT to find the source before treatment
explanation: Septic shock requires the Sepsis Six within 1 hour: cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and IV fluids. Do not delay treatment for imaging.

scenario: A 20-year-old woman faints after seeing blood during a blood test, with a prodrome of light-headedness and sweating, and recovers quickly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cardiac syncope
Vasovagal (reflex) syncope
Orthostatic hypotension
Seizure
Hypoglycaemia
explanation: A prodrome of light-headedness/sweating triggered by a stressful stimulus (needle) with rapid recovery is classic vasovagal (reflex) syncope.

scenario: A 55-year-old man collapses while running, with no prodrome. His father died suddenly at age 50. What is the most important next step?
options: Reassure and discharge
ECG and cardiology assessment for possible cardiac syncope
Tilt-table test
Psychiatric review
CT head
explanation: Exertional syncope with no prodrome and a family history of sudden death suggests a cardiac cause (arrhythmia, HCM) — needs ECG and cardiology assessment.

scenario: A 78-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops sudden pain, pallor, and coldness of his right leg with absent pulses. He has no prior claudication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic limb ischaemia
Acute embolic limb ischaemia
Deep vein thrombosis
Cellulitis
Sciatica
explanation: Sudden onset of a cold, pulseless, painful leg in a patient with AF suggests acute embolic limb ischaemia — a time-critical surgical emergency.

scenario: A patient with an acutely ischaemic leg develops paralysis and paraesthesia. What does this indicate?
options: Mild ischaemia that will resolve
Advanced ischaemia with imminent irreversible damage
Venous congestion
Nerve root compression
Normal finding
explanation: Paralysis and paraesthesia indicate advanced ischaemia with irreversible muscle/nerve damage imminent — urgent revascularisation needed.

scenario: A diabetic patient has a painless punched-out ulcer on the plantar surface of the foot with loss of monofilament sensation. What is the most likely cause?
options: Arterial ischaemia
Venous insufficiency
Neuropathic (diabetic) ulcer
Malignancy
Pressure sore
explanation: A painless plantar ulcer with loss of protective sensation (monofilament) in a diabetic is a neuropathic ulcer.

scenario: A patient with rest pain and an ABPI of 0.4 has a non-healing ulcer on the heel. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wound dressings only
Best medical therapy and vascular surgery referral for revascularisation
Amputation immediately
Antibiotics only
Observation
explanation: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (rest pain, ABPI <0.5, non-healing ulcer) needs best medical therapy plus revascularisation.

scenario: A 30-year-old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill has sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia. Wells score is 5. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: D-dimer and discharge if negative
CTPA (or V/Q) to confirm PE
Chest X-ray only
Antibiotics for pneumonia
Observe for 24 hours
explanation: A high Wells score (>4) with suspected PE warrants direct imaging (CTPA), not D-dimer. Anticoagulate if high probability while awaiting.

scenario: A patient with a suspected massive PE is hypotensive and shocked. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV fluids and observe
Thrombolysis (alteplase)
CTPA before any treatment
LMWH only
Inotropes
explanation: Massive PE with shock/hypotension requires urgent thrombolysis — do not delay for imaging.

scenario: A 70-year-old man with known COPD has an exacerbation with oxygen saturations of 90% on air. What oxygen target should you aim for?
options: No oxygen
explanation: Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD) should be oxygenated to a target of 88-92% to avoid suppressing respiratory drive.

scenario: A patient with acute severe asthma has a silent chest and is becoming drowsy. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Nebulised salbutamol and observe
Call for help — this is a peri-arrest emergency
Chest X-ray
Oral steroids
Discharge with inhalers
explanation: A silent chest with drowsiness in asthma indicates near-fatal asthma — call for help immediately (peri-arrest).

scenario: A patient with COPD and hypercapnic respiratory failure is on oxygen. What is the most appropriate target saturation?
options: No target needed
explanation: COPD patients at risk of hypercapnia should be oxygenated to 88-92% to avoid worsening CO2 retention.

scenario: A patient's oxygen saturations fall to 85% despite a non-rebreathe mask at 15 L/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Increase to 20 L/min
Call for help and consider ABG and the cause of refractory hypoxia
Reduce oxygen
Reassure and recheck in an hour
Give nebulised saline
explanation: Refractory hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen is an emergency — call for help, check ABG, and look for the cause (PE, pneumothorax, shunt).

scenario: An ABG shows pH 7.28, PaCO2 8.0 kPa, HCO3 24. What is the acid-base diagnosis?
options: Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Mixed acidosis
explanation: Low pH (acidaemia) with high PaCO2 and normal HCO3 = respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation).

scenario: An ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 3.5 kPa, HCO3 12, lactate 6. What is the most likely cause?
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap (lactic acidosis)
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Normal
explanation: Low pH with low HCO3 and a high lactate = high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis).

scenario: A patient with renal failure has a potassium of 7.0 mmol/L and ECG shows peaked T waves. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral potassium
IV calcium gluconate, then insulin+dextrose
Observe and recheck
IV fluids only
Stop all potassium-containing food
explanation: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a cardiac emergency — IV calcium gluconate protects the myocardium, then shift K+ with insulin+dextrose.

scenario: A patient on a thiazide diuretic has a potassium of 2.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV calcium gluconate
Oral/IV potassium replacement and review the diuretic
Insulin+dextrose
Nebulised salbutamol
No treatment needed
explanation: Hypokalaemia from diuretics is treated with potassium replacement and review of the causative drug.

scenario: A post-operative patient has urine output of 0.2 mL/kg/h, is tachycardic and hypotensive with dry mucous membranes. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: IV furosemide
IV fluid challenge and reassess
Renal USS
Start dialysis
Restrict fluids
explanation: Pre-renal AKI from hypovolaemia responds to a fluid challenge. Diuretics would worsen pre-renal failure.

scenario: A patient develops anuria (no urine output) after pelvic surgery. What is the most important next step?
options: IV fluids
Check for obstruction (catheter, USS) and renal function
Furosemide
Dialysis
Observe
explanation: Anuria suggests obstruction (post-renal) or severe renal failure — check the catheter, do a renal USS, and assess renal function.

scenario: A patient is hypovolaemic and needs IV fluid resuscitation. Which fluid is most appropriate as first-line?
options: 0.9% saline
Balanced crystalloid (e.g. Hartmann's)
5% dextrose
Colloid (gelatin)
Blood
explanation: Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) are preferred first-line for resuscitation over 0.9% saline (which can cause hyperchloraemic acidosis).

scenario: What is the approximate daily maintenance water requirement for an adult?
options: 10-15 mL/kg/day
25-30 mL/kg/day
50-60 mL/kg/day
100 mL/kg/day
5 mL/kg/day
explanation: Adult maintenance is ~25-30 mL/kg/day of water, with ~1 mmol/kg/day each of Na+ and K+.

scenario: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis and is tachycardic and hypotensive. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral omeprazole and observe
IV access, resuscitation, terlipressin + antibiotics, urgent endoscopy
CT abdomen
Lactulose
Transfusion only
explanation: A variceal bleed in cirrhosis is life-threatening — resuscitate, give terlipressin + antibiotics, and arrange urgent endoscopy for banding.

scenario: A patient with melaena and haemodynamic compromise has a suspected upper GI bleed. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Urgent endoscopy before anything else
Resuscitate with IV access, bloods, fluids/blood, then endoscopy
CT abdomen
Oral iron
Discharge with PPI
explanation: Resuscitate first (IV access, bloods, crossmatch, fluids/blood), then arrange urgent endoscopy. Do not scope an unstable patient.

scenario: A cirrhotic patient develops confusion and asterixis after a GI bleed. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Sedate with a benzodiazepine
Lactulose and treat the precipitant (bleed)
IV antibiotics only
High-protein diet
Observe
explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is treated with lactulose and by treating the precipitant (GI bleed). Avoid sedatives.

scenario: Which of the following is a common precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy?
options: Constipation
Hyperglycaemia
Hypernatraemia
Excess sleep
High potassium
explanation: Constipation (increased ammonia absorption), GI bleed, infection, and electrolyte disturbance are common precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy.

scenario: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops fever and abdominal pain. Ascitic fluid shows neutrophils of 400/mm3. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe
IV antibiotics (cefotaxime) + albumin for SBP
Paracentesis only
Oral antibiotics
Lactulose
explanation: Ascitic neutrophils >250/mm3 = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — IV antibiotics (cefotaxime) + albumin.

scenario: A patient with tense ascites needs a large-volume paracentesis. What should be given alongside to prevent circulatory dysfunction?
options: IV furosemide
IV albumin
IV saline
Oral spironolactone
Nothing
explanation: Large-volume paracentesis (>5 L) should be accompanied by IV albumin to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.

scenario: A patient has jaundice with pale stools, dark urine, and a raised ALP/GGT with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. USS shows dilated bile ducts. What is the most likely cause?
options: Haemolysis
Obstructive jaundice (e.g. gallstone or malignancy)
Viral hepatitis
Alcoholic liver disease
Gilbert's syndrome
explanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with raised ALP/GGT and dilated ducts = obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice.

scenario: A patient has fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Viral hepatitis — supportive care
Cholangitis — IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage
Haemolysis — blood transfusion
Gilbert's — reassure
Pancreatitis — NBM
explanation: Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) = cholangitis, an emergency needing IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP).

scenario: A patient on chemotherapy has a temperature of 38.5°C and a neutrophil count of 0.3 × 10^9/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Paracetamol and observe
Blood cultures then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Wait for culture results before antibiotics
Oral antibiotics
Discharge with advice
explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency — blood cultures then IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for results.

scenario: What defines neutropenic sepsis?
options: Temperature ≥38°C with neutrophils <0.5 × 10^9/L
Any fever with a normal neutrophil count
Temperature >40°C
Neutrophils <1.0 × 10^9/L
Positive blood cultures
explanation: Neutropenic sepsis = fever (≥38°C) or sepsis signs with neutrophils <0.5 × 10^9/L in a patient on chemotherapy/haematological malignancy.

scenario: A young man with haemophilia A presents with a swollen, painful knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Aspirin for pain
Factor VIII replacement + analgesia + rest
Joint aspiration
NSAIDs
Observation only
explanation: Haemarthrosis in haemophilia A is treated with factor VIII replacement, analgesia (avoid aspirin/NSAIDs), and rest.

scenario: Which is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
options: Haemophilia A
Haemophilia B
von Willebrand disease
Factor XI deficiency
Protein C deficiency
explanation: von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, causing mucocutaneous bleeding.

scenario: A patient with metastatic prostate cancer develops new thoracic back pain and leg weakness. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Analgesia and outpatient review
High-dose dexamethasone and urgent MRI whole spine
CT spine
Physiotherapy
Observation
explanation: Suspected malignant spinal cord compression is an emergency — high-dose dexamethasone and urgent MRI whole spine (within 24h).

scenario: Which of the following is a red flag for malignant spinal cord compression?
options: Back pain with a sensory level and bladder dysfunction
Muscle stiffness
Mild backache after exercise
Sciatica
Cervical lymphadenopathy
explanation: Back pain with a sensory level, leg weakness, or bladder/bowel dysfunction in a cancer patient = MSCC until proven otherwise.

scenario: A patient with type 1 diabetes has DKA with a potassium of 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start insulin immediately
Replace potassium before starting insulin
Give IV fluids only
Give sodium bicarbonate
Start metformin
explanation: In DKA, replace potassium before/with insulin — insulin drives K+ into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalaemia.

scenario: A patient with type 2 diabetes has glucose of 38 mmol/L, marked dehydration, but no significant ketosis or acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: DKA
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)
Hypoglycaemia
Lactic acidosis
Sepsis
explanation: Severe hyperglycaemia with dehydration but no significant ketosis/acidosis = HHS, treated with aggressive fluids and cautious insulin.

scenario: A diabetic patient is found unconscious with a glucose of 1.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral glucose tablets
IV 10% glucose (or IM glucagon) and protect the airway
Wait for them to wake
IV insulin
Give a meal
explanation: An unconscious hypoglycaemic patient needs IV glucose (or IM glucagon) with airway protection — not oral treatment.

scenario: What is the threshold for hypoglycaemia in a diabetic patient?
options: <2.0 mmol/L
<4.0 mmol/L
<5.5 mmol/L
<6.0 mmol/L
<7.0 mmol/L
explanation: Hypoglycaemia is defined as glucose <4.0 mmol/L in a diabetic patient.

scenario: A diabetic patient has a deep infected foot ulcer with crepitus and systemic sepsis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral antibiotics and outpatient review
IV antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement
Wound dressings only
Observation
Podiatry referral only
explanation: A necrotising infected diabetic foot with sepsis is a surgical emergency — IV antibiotics and urgent debridement.

scenario: A diabetic patient has a deep foot ulcer and 'probe-to-bone' is positive. What is the most likely complication?
options: Cellulitis
Osteomyelitis
Gangrene
Charcot arthropathy
Venous ulcer
explanation: Probe-to-bone in a diabetic foot ulcer strongly suggests underlying osteomyelitis.

scenario: An elderly patient develops acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Dementia
Delirium
Depression
Schizophrenia
Normal ageing
explanation: Acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention = delirium, common in the acutely ill elderly. Dementia is chronic and progressive.

scenario: Which of the following is a common reversible cause of delirium?
options: Urinary retention
Alzheimer's disease
Huntington's disease
Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Parkinson's disease
explanation: Urinary retention, infection, drugs, constipation, and metabolic disturbance are common reversible causes of delirium.

scenario: An elderly patient falls and is found on the floor for several hours. What complication should you specifically look for?
options: Rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, and pressure injury
Hyperglycaemia
Hypernatraemia
Pneumothorax
Appendicitis
explanation: A 'long lie' (>1h on the floor) risks rhabdomyolysis, hypothermia, and pressure injury.

scenario: An elderly patient on an antihypertensive has recurrent falls and a systolic BP drop of 25 mmHg on standing. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cardiac arrhythmia
Postural (orthostatic) hypotension
Vestibular disorder
Stroke
Anaemia
explanation: A SBP drop ≥20 mmHg on standing = postural hypotension, often drug-induced (antihypertensives) — a common cause of falls.

scenario: A 28-year-old woman of reproductive age presents with lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and collapse. What is the most important initial step?
options: CT abdomen
Pregnancy test and assess for ectopic pregnancy
USS pelvis only
Appendicectomy
Observe
explanation: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain/bleeding/collapse may have a ruptured ectopic — pregnancy test and urgent assessment.

scenario: A woman has a postpartum haemorrhage of 1200 mL. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Observe
Call for help, IV access, fluids/blood, uterotonics, and identify the cause
Oral iron
Discharge
USS only
explanation: PPH is an emergency — call for help, resuscitate, give uterotonics (oxytocin), and identify the cause (4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin).

scenario: A febrile, unwell child has a non-blanching purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Observe for 6 hours
IV antibiotics for suspected meningococcal sepsis
Antihistamines
Topical steroids
Paracetamol and discharge
explanation: Non-blanching purpura + fever/illness = meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — IV antibiotics immediately.

scenario: A patient on a new drug develops widespread blistering with oral mucosal involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate action?
options: Urticaria — antihistamines
Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN — stop the drug and urgent care
Cellulitis — antibiotics
Shingles — antivirals
Scabies — permethrin
explanation: Blistering with mucosal involvement on a drug = SJS/TEN, a medical emergency — stop the culprit drug and urgent specialist care.

scenario: A patient has a temperature of 38.5°C, NEWS2 of 6, and a lactate of 3.5. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Paracetamol and observe
Sepsis Six: cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids within 1 hour
Wait for cultures
CT to find the source first
Discharge with oral antibiotics
explanation: Suspected sepsis with organ dysfunction (NEWS2 ≥5, raised lactate) needs the Sepsis Six within 1 hour — do not delay antibiotics.

scenario: What is the single most important time-critical intervention in sepsis?
options: IV fluids
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Blood cultures
Lactate measurement
Oxygen
explanation: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of suspected sepsis is the most important time-critical intervention.

scenario: A patient is diagnosed with Clostridium difficile. What hand hygiene method is most appropriate?
options: Alcohol hand rub
Soap and water
No hand hygiene needed
Gloves only
Chlorhexidine only
explanation: C. difficile spores are not killed by alcohol hand rub — use soap and water.

scenario: A patient has suspected pulmonary tuberculosis. What precautions are required?
options: Standard precautions only
Airborne precautions (negative pressure, FFP3)
Contact precautions
Droplet precautions
No precautions
explanation: TB is airborne — negative pressure isolation and FFP3 respirator.

scenario: A patient is in pulseless ventricular tachycardia. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Adrenaline first
Defibrillate immediately, then CPR
Amiodarone first
Observe
IV fluids
explanation: Shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT) need immediate defibrillation, then CPR. Don't delay defibrillation for drugs.

scenario: During CPR for PEA, which of the following is a reversible cause to look for?
options: Tension pneumothorax
Hyperglycaemia
Hypernatraemia
Anaemia
Hypothyroidism
explanation: The 4 Ts (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis) and 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, K+, hypothermia) are reversible causes of PEA.

scenario: A patient develops stridor, wheeze, and hypotension after a bee sting. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Oral antihistamine
IM adrenaline 500 mcg, call for help, high-flow oxygen
IV hydrocortisone only
Nebulised salbutamol only
Observe
explanation: Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline (first-line, life-saving), call for help, and high-flow oxygen.

scenario: What is the first-line drug and route for anaphylaxis?
options: IV hydrocortisone
IM adrenaline (anterolateral thigh)
IV chlorphenamine
Nebulised adrenaline
Oral prednisolone
explanation: IM adrenaline 500 mcg (0.5 mL 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh is first-line for anaphylaxis.

scenario: A patient presents 5 hours after a paracetamol overdose. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe
Check paracetamol level and give N-acetylcysteine if indicated
Activated charcoal
Gastric lavage
Discharge
explanation: Paracetamol overdose is treated with N-acetylcysteine if the 4-hour level is above the treatment line (or staggered/late presentation).

scenario: A patient with opioid overdose has respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: IV naloxone and airway support
IV flumazenil
Activated charcoal
Observe
IV diazepam
explanation: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression is treated with naloxone (IV/IM) and airway support.

scenario: A patient 5 days post-bowel surgery develops fever, peritonism, and rising inflammatory markers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Wound infection
Anastomotic leak
Urinary tract infection
Atelectasis
Ileus
explanation: Fever + peritonism days 3-7 after bowel surgery suggests an anastomotic leak — urgent CT/surgery.

scenario: A post-operative patient has abdominal distension, nausea, and absent bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Anastomotic leak
Post-operative ileus
Bleeding
Pneumonia
DVT
explanation: Abdominal distension, nausea, and absent bowel sounds after surgery = post-operative ileus — NBM, NG tube, correct electrolytes, mobilise.

scenario: A post-operative patient has a painful, palpable bladder and cannot pass urine. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe
Catheterise and drain the bladder
IV fluids
Furosemide
Analgesia only
explanation: Acute urinary retention is treated by catheterisation and drainage, then investigating the cause.

scenario: A patient has painless chronic urinary retention with overflow incontinence and a raised creatinine. What is the concern?
options: No concern
High-pressure retention causing renal impairment — urgent drainage
Bladder cancer
Prostatitis
UTI only
explanation: High-pressure chronic retention can cause renal impairment — urgent drainage and renal assessment.

scenario: You realise you have given a patient the wrong dose of insulin. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Do nothing if the patient seems fine
Assess the patient, treat any harm, inform the patient, and report the incident
Hide the error
Wait and see
Blame the nurse
explanation: On a medication error: assess the patient immediately, treat harm, inform the patient, report (datix), and document.

scenario: Which of the following is a key strategy to prevent medication errors?
options: Relying on memory
Checking the '5 rights' (patient, drug, dose, route, time)
Using abbreviations
Verbal orders without confirmation
Skipping allergy checks
explanation: Checking the 5 rights, confirming allergies, and double-checking high-risk drugs prevent medication errors.

scenario: A patient has a NEWS2 of 8. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Recheck in 4 hours
Emergency response — call for help immediately
Routine ward care
Discharge
Increase monitoring only
explanation: NEWS2 ≥7 triggers an emergency response — call for help immediately.

scenario: A NEWS2 of 5 or more should prompt what additional action?
options: Nothing
Screening for sepsis
Immediate ICU admission
Discharge
Psychiatric review
explanation: NEWS2 ≥5 is a trigger for sepsis screening.

scenario: A patient with a central line develops a fever. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe
Blood cultures (peripheral + line) and consider removing the line
Remove the line without cultures
Antibiotics only
USS the line
explanation: Suspected line sepsis: take blood cultures (peripheral and line), consider removing the line, and treat with antibiotics.

scenario: A patient with a central line suddenly collapses with hypoxia. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Observe
Clamp the line, head-down/left lateral position, 100% oxygen
Remove the line
IV fluids
USS the line
explanation: Sudden collapse with a central line suggests air embolism — clamp the line, position head-down/left lateral, and give 100% oxygen.

scenario: A patient with COVID-19 pneumonia needs oxygen. What is the most appropriate oxygen target?
options: 94-98% (88-92% if hypercapnia risk)
No target
explanation: Target 94-98% for most, 88-92% if at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.

scenario: Which treatment is indicated for a COVID-19 patient who requires oxygen?
options: Dexamethasone
Antibiotics routinely
No treatment
High-dose steroids for all
Ibuprofen
explanation: Dexamethasone is indicated for COVID-19 patients who require oxygen (reduces mortality).
